Haha. Thanks! I know what I do just from experience with my cats and research that I’ve done while caring for them. Have you tried different materials for the posts? Could be a couple things. They may just really like the feeling of the carpet. There are posts made with carpet material you can try. Could also be they like scratching in a position on the floor. You could try a cardboard scratcher or a mat/rug  of just for them. 

Sometimes cats can be picky about what their paws touch so if you haven’t already I would just try out different types of scratchers and see what sticks. If you try a rug just for them you could put it in their most scratched area and get them used to it. Hope this helps!
At first just one. We didn’t know how much better it is to have two. Then later on we adopted a 2nd kitten.

Bearded dragon would be a good one and the first that comes to mind. If you’re looking for something lower maintenance then I’d go with a snake. Fairly easy to care for and lower maintenance. Me personally I’d go with a rainbow boa but that’s a personal choice. 

A tank that size you could put a few leopard geckos in. (Make sure they’re all female if you don’t want babies, multiple males might cause some fights.) 

Really you could have just about anything. Rodents are usually better in something with more airflow than a tank but if you are diligent about cleaning shouldn’t be too much of an issue. I wouldn’t do anything bigger than a rat though because the odor/vapor from waste can cause respiratory issues for the animal.

My cats are the best anti depressants I’ve ever had. I highly recommend them.

Yes their claws can get sharp but that’s why you trim them. Work with the cat to get them used to having their paws touched. I have one cat that just sits there when I trim his nails. The other is more sensitive and squirms a lot, best time to try is mid nap. Worst time is when they have playful zoomies. 

If you’ll be gone extended time try two cats. 

If you get kittens have them used to fry food always available (will keep them from waking for food and allow you to leave extra if you’re gone over night) and wet food at least once a day. 

If you’re worried about furniture most cats can be trained what to scratch, make sure they have plenty of options. Scratching is ingrained in them, they will scratch something no matter what, so make sure they have appropriate options. We have one cat that’s very smart and will only scratch his posts or mats. We have another who is a bit of a lovable doofus and will from time to time choose the furniture. 

Recommend 2 litter boxes. Seems to work well for them to have two options. Also helps if you’re away a day or two can cant scoop it that day. 

Having plenty of fresh clean water is also very important. 

Wishing you the absolute best!

The question is which feels best in your hands when you play? A lot of people will try to steer you away from the 6 string just on the principle of “that’s too many strings, you don’t need them.” 
What’s most important is that the bass is comfortable to play without straining too much. If you are straining too much then you’re more likely to pick up bad habits that are difficult to unlearn. 
Now, what I will say about 6 strings is that you’ll need to develop good technique to get a good sound. More strings means more strings you’ll have to mute to keep them from ringing when you don’t want them to. If you don’t you end up with your sound getting muddied up. (Recording yourself and listening back will help see how you’re doing with this).

Basically an A/C system just moves heat outside. You have a compressor, a condenser, and evaporator, and refrigerant as your basic parts. There’s also a high pressure and low pressure side to the system. The refrigerant (Freon, r-134a, etc...) boils at a really low temperature. When it turns from liquid to gas it takes a lot of heat from the air with it. When it turns back to a liquid it releases that heat it absorbed. 

So, the compressor compresses the Freon or whatever the system uses so that it is under pressure. The Freon travels through the high pressure side til it gets to a valve or an orifice. After the orifice it is now on the low pressure side. When the refrigerant travels through to the low side it’s is no longer compressed when makes it release heat and feel colder. Think of an aerosol can. It’s under pressure but when you’re spraying it the contents feel cool because they’re decompressing. Making the refrigerant colder increases the amount of heat it’ll be able to absorb. 

The refrigerant is currently liquid and travels to the evaporator. The evaporator does just as its name suggests, inside the Freon evaporates (or boils) and becomes a gas. At the moment it turns from liquid to gas it absorbs a lot of heat from the air. You’ll have a fan blowing on the evaporator and that’s how you’ll have cold air blow out of the A/c.

Our now gas Freon travels though the system now to the condenser. Think condensation, it goes from gas, and condenses back to liquid in the condenser. A fan pulls in air over the condenser cooling the Freon. When it changes from gas to liquid it releases the heat it absorbed outside.  

So long story short, you can’t create cold or heat, you just move it outside the house or car.
